en: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya, Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm, translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlabhadra of India during the Tang Dynasty.
At that time, Lady Māyā again addressed the youth Sudhana, saying: "Good man! In..."

In this world, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there is a king named Samprajanya. The king has a daughter named Devendraprabhā. Go to her and ask: how does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?

Then the youth Sudhana, respectfully receiving his instruction, prostrated himself with his head at [the master's] feet, circumambulated him countless times, and, gazing up at him with longing and veneration, withdrew while walking backward.
She then proceeded to the celestial palace, where she beheld that maiden. She prostrated at her feet, circumambulated her, and stood before her with palms joined, saying:
"Noble Lady!
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path."
"I have heard that the Noble One is skilled at providing instruction;
I pray that you will speak for me. The goddess replied, "Good son!
I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called "Pure Adornment of Unobstructed Mindfulness. Good son!
I recall that in the past, there was a most excellent eon named Blue Lotus, during which I made offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.

From the time those Tathāgatas first left the household life until their passing, I attended to them all, protecting, honoring, and making offerings to them; I constructed monasteries and provided all necessary articles.

Furthermore, regarding those Buddhas—from the time they dwelt in their mothers’ wombs as Bodhisattvas, to their birth, their taking of seven steps, their uttering the great lion’s roar, their dwelling in the palace during their youth, their proceeding toward the Bodhi tree to attain perfect enlightenment, and their turning the wheel of the true Dharma while manifesting Buddha-miracles to teach, transform, and subdue sentient beings—I clearly remember all such deeds performed throughout their careers, from their first aspiration until the end of the Dharma, without exception; they are ever present before me, held in mind and never forgotten.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past, during an eon named Good Ground (*Sudhara*), I made offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges Rivers;
again, in a past eon named Wondrous Virtue (*Guna-vyuha*), I made offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in a single Buddha-world;
and again, in an eon named Non-attainment (*Anupalabdhi*), I made offerings to eighty-four billion hundred thousand nayutas of Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, there was an eon named Good Light, in which I made offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa;
another eon named Immeasurable Light, in which I made offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in twenty Ganges Rivers;
and another eon named Virtue of Diligence, in which I made offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River.
Furthermore, there was an eon named Subhāṣita (Good Compassion), in which I made offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in eighty Ganges Rivers;
another eon named Vijaya-vihāra (Victorious Roaming), in which I made offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in sixty Ganges Rivers;
and another eon named Sucandra (Wondrous Moon), in which I made offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in seventy Ganges Rivers.
"Good son!

Thus, as I recall kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have never ceased to attend upon all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. From all those Tathāgatas, I heard this Bodhisattva liberation of 'Unobstructed Mindfulness and Pure Adornment,' which I have upheld, practiced, and entered into in accordance with it, without interruption."

Thus, regarding all the Tathāgatas of previous kalpas—from their initial stage as bodhisattvas until the exhaustion of the Dharma—I have, through the power of my liberation of pure adornment, recollected all their supernatural transformations; they appear clearly before me, and I maintain and practice them accordingly, never once becoming weary or negligent.
"Good son!

I only know this liberation of unimpeded mindfulness and purity. As for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, who have emerged from the night of birth and death, who are brilliantly clear and penetrating, who are forever free from the darkness of ignorance, who never fall into stupor or sleep, whose minds are free from all hindrances, whose physical conduct is light and tranquil, who clearly and purely awaken to the nature of all phenomena, and who, having accomplished the Ten Powers, enlighten all living beings—how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?"
"Noble son!
In the city of Kapilavastu, there is a teacher of youths named Viśvāmitra. Go to him and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?'"

At that time, because he had heard the Dharma, the youth Sudhana felt joy in body and mind; his inconceivable roots of goodness flowed forth and expanded. He prostrated himself at the feet of the Lord of Heaven’s Light, circumambulated him countless times, and departing with longing and reverence, descended from the celestial palace and gradually headed toward that city.
He went to the place where Samantabhadra was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence.
He addressed him, saying: "Noble One!
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path."
"I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction;
I pray that you will speak for me. Viśvāmitra replied, "Noble son!..."
"Here is a youth named Śāriputra, who studies the bodhisattva’s knowledge of letters; you should question him, and he will explain it to you.
Thereupon, Sudhana went to his place, prostrated himself with his head at his feet in reverence, stood to one side, and said:
"Noble One!..."
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction;
I pray that you will speak for me. Then the youth said to Sudhana:
"O son of good family!
I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called "Skillful Knowledge of All Arts. I constantly chant and maintain the fundamental syllables that enter this liberation.
When chanting the syllable *A*, I enter a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Distinctive Realms of Bodhisattva Majestic Virtue.
When chanting the syllable *Ra*, I enter a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Supreme and Boundless Equality of One Flavor."
When pronouncing the syllable *pa*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Non-differentiated Character of the Dharma-realm.
When pronouncing the syllable *ca*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Universal Wheel that Severs All Distinctions.
When pronouncing the syllable *ta*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Attaining the Supportless and Unsurpassed."
When pronouncing the syllable *la*, one enters a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "Stainless Detachment from Reliance.
When pronouncing the syllable *ḍa* (pronounced like *tu* with a retroflex *ḍ*), one enters a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "The Practice of Non-retrogression.
When pronouncing the syllable *ba*, one enters a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "The Diamond Seat."
When pronouncing the syllable *ḍa*, one enters a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "Universal Wheel";
when pronouncing the syllable *śa*, one enters a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "Ocean Treasury";
when pronouncing the syllable *tha*, one enters a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "Universally Born and Peacefully Abiding."
When pronouncing the syllable *na*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Perfectly Round Light";
when pronouncing the syllable *ya*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Accumulation of Distinctions";
when pronouncing the syllable *ṣṭha*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universal Radiance that Quells All Afflictions."
When pronouncing the syllable KA, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Single Flavor of Differentiation.
When pronouncing the syllable VA, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Pouring Down of the Rain of Dharma.
When pronouncing the syllable MA, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Great Torrent Rushing Amidst Simultaneously Arrayed Peaks."
When pronouncing the syllable GA, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universally Established Above";
when pronouncing the syllable STHA, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Treasury of True Suchness, Pervasive and Equal";
when pronouncing the syllable DZA, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Entering the Purification of the Ocean of Worlds."
When pronouncing the syllable *śi*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Adornment of Right Mindfulness of All Buddhas";
when pronouncing the syllable *ḍha*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Observing the Perfect Accumulation of Dharmas";
when pronouncing the syllable *ṣa*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Light of the Wheel of Instruction of All Buddhas."
When pronouncing the syllable *kha*, one enters a door of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Treasury of Manifest Wisdom for Purifying the Ground of Causation.
When pronouncing the syllable *kṣa*, one enters a door of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Treasury that Calms the Ocean of All Karmas.
When pronouncing the syllable *stā*, one enters a door of Prajñāpāramitā called "Dispelling All Obscurations of Delusion to Open Pure Radiance."
When pronouncing the syllable *raṅ*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Cause for Awakening to the World.
When pronouncing the syllable *pha*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Wheel of Wisdom that Severs Birth and Death.
When pronouncing the syllable *ba*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "All Palaces Fully Adorned."
When pronouncing the syllable *cha*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Fulfillment of Each Individual Treasury of Ethical Discipline through Practice.
When pronouncing the syllable *sama*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Manifestly Beholding All Buddhas Throughout the Ten Directions.

When pronouncing the syllable *hava*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Observing All Beings Without Conditions and Gathering Them Through Skillful Means to Cause Them to Arise in the Ocean-Treasury."
When pronouncing the syllable *ha*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Cultivating Entry into the Ocean of All Meritorious Qualities.
When pronouncing the syllable *ga*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Firm Oceanic Treasury that Sustains the Clouds of All Dharmas.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Manifest Presence of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions According to One's Vows."
When pronouncing the syllable *ṇa*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Assembly of Billions of Syllables within the Immutable Syllable-Wheel.
When pronouncing the syllable *spha*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Ultimate Place for Transforming Sentient Beings.

When pronouncing the syllable *ska*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Radiant Wheel of Unattached and Unobstructed Understanding that Illuminates Everywhere through the Fulfillment of All Stages."
When pronouncing the syllable *ja*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Proclaiming the Realm of All Buddha-Dharmas.
When pronouncing the syllable *ta-sa*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Universal Roar of the Thunder of All Space-like Dharmas.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭha* (pronounced with the retroflex *ṭ*), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Bright Lamp that Illuminates the Deluded Consciousnesses as Selfless."
When pronouncing the syllable *ḍha*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Treasury from which All Dharma Wheels Are Born.
Son of good family!

When I pronounce such fundamental syllables for entering all liberations, with these forty-two gates of Prajñāpāramitā as the foremost, one enters immeasurable and innumerable gates of Prajñāpāramitā.
“Good son!

I know only this bodhisattva liberation of ‘Skillfully Knowing All Arts. As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to reach the further shore through wisdom regarding all mundane and supramundane skillful dharmas, who comprehensively master various methods and diverse arts without omission, who possess profound understanding of writing, mathematics, and the aggregates, and who excel in medicine, incantations, and esoteric arts to effectively treat all manner of illnesses—[I do not know their ways].”

There are sentient beings who are possessed by ghosts and demons, afflicted by resentment and malevolent incantations, affected by the portents of evil stars, pursued by wandering corpses, or suffering from epilepsy, emaciation, and various other ailments; [this mantra] can save them all and cause them to be fully healed.

Furthermore, he skillfully distinguishes gold, silver, pearls, shells, coral, lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, musaragalva, karketana, and all other such treasures; he knows their origins, their diverse varieties, and their respective values. Whether it be villages, camps, towns, small or large cities, palaces, gardens, mountain crags, springs, marshes, or any dwelling place of human beings, the Bodhisattva is able to provide protection and guidance for them all according to their specific circumstances.

Furthermore, he skillfully observed celestial phenomena and terrestrial geography, the physiognomy of men and their auspicious or inauspicious signs, the cries of birds and beasts, the formations of clouds and mists and seasonal shifts, the abundance or scarcity of crops, and the security or peril of kingdoms; regarding all such worldly arts and crafts, there were none in which he was not thoroughly practiced, having mastered them to their very source and foundation.

Furthermore, they are able to discern the supramundane dharmas, correctly defining their names and clarifying their meanings; they observe their essential natures and characteristics and practice in accordance with them. Their wisdom enters therein, free from doubt and hindrance, free from ignorance and dullness, free from sorrow and affliction, and free from despondency; there is nothing they do not directly realize.
How then could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
Son of good family!

In this kingdom of Magadha, there is a village, and within it is a city named Bhaddana. There dwells a laywoman (upāsikā) named Bhadrottamā. Go to her and ask: how does a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then the youth Sudhana paid homage at the feet of Viśvāmitra by touching his head to them, circumambulated him countless times, and departed with longing and veneration.
Heading toward the city of the village, he arrived at the place of Bhadrasena; prostrating at his feet and circumambulating him, he stood to one side with palms joined in reverence and said:
"Noble One!"
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practices and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction;
I pray that you will speak for me. Bhadrajaya replied, "Good son!
I have attained a bodhisattva dharma-gate called the "Dharma-Seat Without Dependence. Having realized it for myself, I further explain it to others.

Furthermore, I have attained the Inexhaustible Samādhi; it is not that this samādhi-dharma itself is either exhaustible or inexhaustible, but because it can give rise to the inexhaustible eye of the nature of all-knowledge, and can also give rise to the ear of the nature of all-knowledge.
Because they are inexhaustible, they can further give rise to the inexhaustible nature of all-knowledge of the nose;

because they are inexhaustible, they can further give rise to the inexhaustible nature of all-knowledge of the tongue; because they are inexhaustible, they can further give rise to the inexhaustible nature of all-knowledge of the body;
because they are inexhaustible, they can further give rise to the inexhaustible nature of all-knowledge of the mind; and they can further give rise to one...
Because the nature of all-knowledge gives rise to the inexhaustibility of various wisdoms and luminosities;

because it can give rise to the inexhaustibility of the all-pervading supernormal powers of the nature of all-knowledge; because it can give rise to the inexhaustibility of immeasurable merits like the waves and billows of the ocean from the nature of all-knowledge;
and because it can give rise to the light that pervades the world from the nature of all-knowledge.
Because it is inexhaustible. Good son!
I know only this Dharma-gate of the Bodhimanda of Non-Reliance; as for the meritorious practices of non-attachment of all the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, how could I possibly know or explain them all?
"Good son!

To the south there is a city named Kṣema; therein dwells an elder named Dṛḍhavimukti. You should go and ask him: 'How does a bodhisattva study the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path?'"
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Bhadrasena, circumambulated him countless times, and gazing up at him with longing and devotion, took his leave and traveled south.
Upon reaching that city, he went to the householder’s residence, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and standing to one side with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:
"Noble One!
I have already set my mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I have heard that the Noble One is skilled at providing instruction;
I pray that you will speak for me. The elder replied, "Good son!

I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called "Unattached Pure Mindfulness. Since I first attained this liberation, my aspirations regarding the Dharma have been fulfilled, and I no longer harbor any further expectations toward the Buddhas of the ten directions.
"Noble son!

I know only this liberation of pure mindfulness. As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the fearless great lion’s roar and dwell securely in a vast and lofty accumulation of merit and wisdom—how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?"
"Good son!
In this very city there is an elder named Candraprabha (Moonlight). At that elder’s residence, there is always a radiant light.
Go to him and ask: how does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?"
Then the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Dṛḍhamati, circumambulated him countless times, and took his leave to depart.
He went to the place where Candracchattra was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence, saying:
"Noble One!
I have already set my mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I have heard that the Holy One is skilled at providing instruction;
I pray that you will speak for me. Candracchattra replied, "Noble son!
I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called "Pure Wisdom Radiance. Noble son!

I know only this liberation of the light of wisdom; as for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have realized immeasurable dharma-gates of liberation, how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
"Good son!

To the south of here, there is a city named Utpala. In it dwells an elder named Ajitasena. Go to him and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?'"
At that time, Sudhana paid homage at the feet of Candracchattra, circumambulated him countless times, and departed with longing and veneration.
Gradually heading toward that city, he arrived at the householder’s residence, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence, saying:
"Noble One!"
I have already set my mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I have heard that the Holy One is skilled at providing instruction and guidance;
I pray that you will speak for me. The elder replied, "Good son!..."
I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called "Inexhaustible Aspect. Having realized this bodhisattva liberation, I behold immeasurable buddhas and obtain an inexhaustible treasury.
"Good son!

I know only this liberation of inexhaustible marks. As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained infinite wisdom and unimpeded eloquence—how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?"
"Noble son!

To the south of this city, there is a village named Dharma. In that village, there is a brahmin named Śivivara; go to him and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?'"
Then the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Anābhibhūsenāpati, circumambulated him countless times, and departed with longing and reverence.
Traveling south by stages, he arrived at that village, saw Śibi Jyeṣṭha, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and stood to one side with palms joined in respect, saying:
"Noble One!
I have already set my mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I have heard that the Holy One is well able to provide instruction;
I pray that you will speak for me. The Brahmin replied, "Noble son!"

I have attained a bodhisattva dharma-gate called "Speech of Sincere Vows. Because of this speech, all bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future shall never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they have not regressed, do not currently regress, and will not regress.
"Noble son!
Because I abide in speech of truthful resolve, whatever I do according to my will is never not fulfilled.
Noble son!"

I know only this Dharma-gate of truthful speech; as for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, who act in accordance with their words of sincere vows, whose conduct never deviates from their practice, and whose speech is invariably truthful and never false—since immeasurable merit arises therefrom, how could I possibly know or speak of it?
"Good son!

To the south of here there is a city named Sumanāmukha. There dwells a youth named Guṇākara and a maiden named Guṇavatī. Go to them and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?'"
At that time, the youth Sudhana, out of deep reverence for the Dharma, prostrated at the feet of the brahmin, circumambulated him countless times, and departed with longing and veneration.

Traveling south by stages, he arrived at that city, where he saw the boy and the girl. He prostrated at their feet, completed his circumambulations, and then, with palms joined before them, spoke these words:
"Noble Ones!"
I have already set my mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I only pray that you will have compassion for me and explain this to me. Then the boy and girl said to Sudhana: "Good man!

We have realized the bodhisattva liberation called 'Abiding as an Illusion. By means of this pure wisdom, we observe that all worlds abide as illusions, because they are produced by causes and conditions."
All sentient beings abide as illusions, for they arise from karma and afflictions;
all phenomena abide as illusions, for they are produced through the successive conditions of ignorance, craving for existence, and so forth;
all three realms abide as illusions, for they are born of inverted cognition.
All sentient beings—birth, death, aging, sickness, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—are illusory abodes, for they are produced by false conceptualization;
all lands are illusory abodes, for they are manifested by the inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, the inversion of view, and ignorance;
all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are illusory abodes, for they are constituted by the discrimination of knowledge and abandonment.

All bodhisattvas abide as illusions, for they are accomplished through their superior wisdom-mind that is able to self-discipline and transform sentient beings, as well as through their various practices and vows;
likewise, all assemblies of bodhisattvas, their transformations and disciplines, and all their activities abide as illusions, for they are comprised and accomplished by means of vows and wisdom.
"Good son! The self-nature of illusory phenomena is inconceivable. Good son!"

We two can only know this liberation of the bodhisattva; as for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have skillfully entered the illusory net of infinite phenomena, how could we possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
When the boy and girl had thus spoken of their own liberation, by the power of their inconceivable roots of goodness, the body of Sudhana became supple and radiant.
The Scripture of the Flower Ornament of the Great Vaipulya Buddha, Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm, Scroll One.
